extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, judges, agency lawyers, and practitioners concerned with rulemaking and APA notice-and-comment procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria for when agencies may invoke the APA 'good cause' exception to adopt interim final rules (IFRs), and for how courts should review IFRs and any resulting final rules (FFRs). Focuses on procedural legitimacy, effects on participation, path dependence, bias, and appropriate remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sunset provision as safeguard
rubrics_metrics.description: An IFR should include a sunset provision to prevent agencies from issuing IFRs they never intend to finalize as a means of undermining judicial review and legislative oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sunset provision changes the default outcome if the rulemaking lapses (instead of allowing the IFR to persist indefinitely). Requiring a sunset provision is consistent with Vermont Yankee to the extent a court finds it necessary to ensure the agency invocation of the exception meets the criteria set out in the APA. Without a sunset provision, agencies might issue IFRs to escape notice-and-comment permanently; courts can require sunsets to make APA procedures meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating inaction (allowing IFR to sunset) as reviewable agency action
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever action or non-action the agency takes regarding finalizing the rule (including allowing an IFR to lapse/sunset) should be considered final agency action subject to judicial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When finalizing an IFR the agency has three choices—adopt an amendment to the IFR as an FFR, adopt the IFR as the FFR, or allow the rule to revert to the prior regulation—and courts should require the agency to defend its ultimate decision regardless of which outcome it chooses. The APA defines 'agency action' to include failures to act (5 U.S.C. §551(13)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit IFRs to situations where they are a good substitute for a NOPR
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should limit interim final rulemaking to those situations where an IFR is an appropriate or good substitute for issuing a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NOPR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because an IFR may be an imperfect substitute for a NOPR (it may alter comments, create path dependencies, or cause bias), courts should assess whether the IFR meaningfully changes the rulemaking process or outcome and restrict use of IFRs where they are not an adequate substitute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approaches to reviewing FFRs that originate from IFRs (categorical invalidity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some courts categorically reject any final rule that results from an IFR the court finds procedurally invalid under the good cause exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These courts fear that allowing FFRs to survive invalid IFRs would permit agencies to substitute IFRs for most rulemakings and 'make §553 virtually unenforceable.' Examples: U.S. Steel Corp. v. EPA; Sharon Steel Corp.; Buschmann.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approaches to reviewing FFRs that originate from IFRs (categorical acceptance / harmless error)
rubrics_metrics.description: Other courts treat an IFR-origin FFR as procedurally legitimate when the use of an IFR is harmless error—that is, the error had 'no bearing on the procedure used or substance of the [ultimate] decision reached.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harmless-error assessments (e.g., Little Sisters of the Poor) require courts to determine whether the use of an IFR detrimentally affected the decision-making process (e.g., altered comments or biased the agency). If not, courts may affirm the FFR even if the IFR did not strictly comply with prepromulgation notice-and-comment requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing effect of IFRs on public comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether issuing an IFR (versus a NOPR) changes the likelihood, quantity, or quality of comments the agency receives and whether that change meaningfully affected the rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments run both ways: issuance of an IFR may discourage comments because stakeholders think the rule is already cemented, or it may increase and improve commenting by making the rule 'real' and educating stakeholders (experimental/pilot effect). There are no conclusive data; courts should examine the record rather than assume postpromulgation comments are inadequate substitutes for prepromulgation notice-and-comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid issuing IFRs that create inefficient path dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency should hesitate to adopt an IFR when the interim rule will require substantial, irreversible investments by regulated parties that could be wasted if a better FFR is later adopted—because of inefficient path dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Path dependence occurs when initial regulation stimulates specific investments or settled expectations that make later adoption of the superior rule inefficient. Numeric balancing (weighing benefits of immediate implementation against the loss from foreclosing better future options) should guide courts: avoid IFRs that induce significant sunk investments unless the interim rule promises overwhelming net benefits over the status quo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing delay costs against lost opportunity costs
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering whether an IFR is justified, weigh the benefits of accelerating implementation (avoiding delay) against the benefits that might be lost if a superior rule would have been adopted after full notice-and-comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article provides numerical examples showing how a one-year acceleration can sometimes outweigh the incremental benefit of a later-adopted ideal rule; courts should analyze the magnitude and duration of benefits and costs to decide whether skipping notice-and-comment is warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review when IFR caused path dependence but FFR is best available
rubrics_metrics.description: If an agency issues an IFR that causes inefficient path dependence but then adopts the best FFR given the new circumstances, the court should ignore the invalidity of the IFR and review the FFR as if it resulted from traditional prepromulgation notice-and-comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once the industry has implemented an IFR and path dependence has occurred, the most efficient forward-looking rule may differ from the ex ante ideal, so remedial reversal of the FFR may not improve welfare; courts should therefore evaluate the FFR on its merits rather than automatically voiding it because of the prior IFR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ameliorating confirmation bias in agency decisionmaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should be attentive to confirmation bias: the adoption of an IFR may bias agency staff and decisionmakers toward reaffirming the initial choice and discounting disconfirming evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirmation bias can manifest as searching for confirming evidence more than disconfirming evidence and discounting counterevidence. Whether an IFR increases bias may depend on cognitive factors such as whether issuing an IFR required more or less staff investment than issuing a NOPR. Courts should be alert to signs of biased information search and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-mind (responsiveness) standard and indicia of receptivity to comments
rubrics_metrics.description: When an IFR is challenged, courts may apply an 'open mind' standard and look for indicia that the agency remained receptive to change during postpromulgation comment: whether the agency actually incorporated changes reflecting comments and whether it engaged in careful, searching consideration of comments (especially by discussing them in the preamble).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: D.C. Circuit practice looks to (1) actual incorporation of comment-driven changes into the FFR and (2) explicit, careful discussion of comments in the preamble. However, courts should be wary that agencies can manipulate these indicia (e.g., making superficial changes or drafting preambles that simulate consideration). The burden to rebut the presumption that the agency had made up its mind rests on the agency; it must make a 'compelling showing' that its mind remained open.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about formalistic indicators of openness
rubrics_metrics.description: Because courts' specified criteria for openness can be gamed, judges should probe beyond formal indicators (like minor changes or preamble discussions) to detect whether the agency truly remained receptive to contrary evidence and argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies might include inconsequential changes or run through comment-by-comment preamble discussions without genuine receptivity. Courts should examine the substance of changes and the quality of engagement with comments rather than rely solely on checklist indicators.
